title: When the Winter Sings
premise: Wren Blackwood, a rationalist pest controller, is hired to deal with 'something with fingerprints' at their late grandmother's house in Hollow Creek, where every photograph now shows an extra empty chair and the townsfolk count aloud at dusk. Wren discovers the house is a threshold being reclaimed by a presence that collects the forgotten, adding each family member to its count one by one as they appear in old photos. Refusing to believe even as siblings and cousins vanish from the present into the pictures, Wren must choose between the duty of silence their grandmother's will demands and the found family of neighbors who help them fight. In the end, Wren breaks the count by giving the presence a name and a memory of love instead of fear, trading their own place in the photographs to pull everyone else out—leaving one chair forever occupied, and Wren remembered only by those who loved them.
about_author: E. M. Marchetti is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed estate photographs in rural New England. They write horror about houses that remember better than people do.

chapters.title: The Call Comes at Dusk
chapters.summary: POV Wren. A letter arrives requesting pest control at the Blackwood family house—signed in grandma's handwriting, dated three years after her death. Wren drives out expecting squatters or a prank, finding dust-free rooms and faint handprints on the inside of sealed windows. The emotional beat: stubborn skepticism masking grief they never processed.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Cataloguing the house for infestation, Wren photographs the family portraits for insurance—and every image now contains an extra wooden chair no one remembers owning. Their cousin Odette confirms it over the phone, voice shaking: her copies changed too. Beat: the first crack in disbelief, dread arriving through something as mundane as furniture.

chapters.title: The Counting Hour
chapters.summary: POV Wren. At dusk, voices drift from the woods counting upward—one, two, three—stopping just short of the family's number. Neighbor Ruthie Pell, an elderly woman grandma trusted, explains the local rule: never answer, never be counted, stay invisible. Beat: Wren learns the town has survived by forgetting, and forgetting is a form of complicity.

chapters.title: What Grandma Left Locked
chapters.summary: POV Wren, with flashbacks in grandma's voice via letters. Behind a false wall, Wren finds grandma's research: decades of photographs, each generation gaining chairs, each disappearance matching a name scratched out of the family Bible. Beat: horror reframed as inheritance—grandma didn't disbelieve; she bargained, and the bill is due.

chapters.title: Odette Stops Answering
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Cousin Odette arrives to help and begins sleepwalking toward the woods, murmuring numbers. Her phone photos show her seated in the extra chair, smiling. When she vanishes mid-sentence, only her coat remains, folded neatly. Beat: guilt ignites into urgency—the count is personal now, and Wren was warned.

chapters.title: The Family We Chose
chapters.summary: POV alternating Wren and Ruthie. Wren rallies the neighbors Ruthie calls 'the left-behinds'—people the presence passed over because no one remembered them. Together they realize the thing feeds on being forgotten, and the forgotten are immune. Beat: found family becomes strategy; love becomes a weapon disguised as loyalty.

chapters.title: Photographs of the Missing
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Inside the newest photos, the vanished sit in the chair, aging years per day, mouths moving silently. Lip-reading Odette's final frame yields three words: 'Say my name.' Wren understands the count can be broken by remembrance—but speaking a counted name aloud invites the counter closer. Beat: hope with teeth.

chapters.title: The House Turns Its Face
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The house itself begins participating: doors rearranging, walls displaying every photo at once, the counting audible inside the plaster. Ruthie is taken answering a knock in grandma's voice. Wren, alone among strangers-turned-allies, nearly answers the next knock themselves. Beat: climax pressure—duty says hide, love says open the door.

chapters.title: Naming the Unnamed
chapters.summary: POV Wren, climax. At the counting hour, Wren walks into the woods carrying grandma's album and speaks the presence's true name—a firstborn Blackwood erased from every record, forgotten so thoroughly it became hunger. Wren offers what it always wanted: to be remembered, grieved, loved. The count falters. Beat: love against duty, made literal.

chapters.title: When the Winter Sings
chapters.summary: POV Ruthie, epilogue. Spring comes to Hollow Creek. The vanished return, dazed but whole, except Wren—who appears in no photograph, lives in no record, remembered only by the people who choose to say their name daily. The extra chair remains by the fire, occupied at dusk by something that finally rests. Beat: bittersweet resolution—invisibility chosen freely, family kept by memory.
